lede: Logarithms turn multiplying into adding and powers into multiplying. Three short laws do all of it, and they work in both directions: they squeeze several logarithms into one, or open one out into several. Almost every logarithm question on the paper is one of the three, used one way or the other.
can: Combine several logarithms into a single logarithm with the three laws
Expand one logarithm into separate logarithms, coefficients and all
Turn a constant into a logarithm, and read log P = log Q as P = Q

text: Three laws that work both ways

md:
A logarithm is an index, and indices already obey rules: multiply two powers and the indices add. The laws of logarithms are those index rules, written the other way up.
That is why there are only three of them, and why each one can be used forwards to squeeze logarithms together or backwards to open one out. Which direction you need is the whole of the question.

alt: The three laws written out: added logarithms multiply inside, subtracted logarithms divide inside, and a number in front becomes a power.

prompt: One tap to begin. In the three laws shown above, what happens inside the logarithm when two logarithms are added?
explain: $\log a + \log b = \log(ab)$. Adding outside means multiplying inside, which is the index rule read backwards.

md:
$\log a + \log b = \log(ab)$. Not $\log(a + b)$: the plus sign is outside the logarithm, and it changes to a times when it goes in.
You can check any law on numbers, which is worth doing once so you never doubt it. $\log 4 + \log 25$ is $0.602 + 1.398 = 2$, and $\log(4 \times 25) = \log 100 = 2$ as well.

alt: The product law checked on numbers: log 4 plus log 25 equals log 100, which is 2.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 158' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The product law checked on numbers: log 4 plus log 25 equals log 100, which is 2'><title>The product law checked on numbers: log 4 plus log 25 equals log 100, which is 2</title><path d='M 14 16 L 14 118' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 14 16 L 24 16 M 14 118 L 24 118' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><text x='28' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log 4 + log 25</text><text x='330' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>two logarithms added</text><rect x='18' y='47' width='290' height='26' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.09'/><text x='28' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log(4 x 25)</text><text x='330' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the product law</text><text x='28' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log 100 = 2</text><text x='330' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>and 0.602 + 1.398 = 2 as well</text><text x='290' y='150' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>the law is not a rule to trust, it is a fact you can check</text></svg>
caption: Added outside, multiplied inside.

title: Why adding turns into multiplying
md: A logarithm is an index. Multiplying $10^{p}$ by $10^{q}$ gives $10^{p + q}$, so the indices add when the numbers multiply. Read that backwards and the logarithms add when their arguments multiply.

prompt: Using the product law shown above, what is $\log 5 + \log 6$ as a single logarithm?
explain: Adding the logarithms multiplies the numbers inside, so it is $\log 30$. Writing $\log 11$ adds them inside, which is the most reported misuse of this law.

md:
$\log a - \log b = \log\frac{a}{b}$. The minus goes in and becomes a division.
The trap here is dividing the two logarithms instead: $\frac{\log a}{\log b}$ is a completely different number, and it is not the logarithm of anything in the question. $\log 100 - \log 4 = \log 25$, while $\log 100 \div \log 4$ is about $3.321928$.

alt: The quotient law checked on numbers: log 100 minus log 4 equals log 25, and dividing the two logarithms gives something else entirely.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 158' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The quotient law checked on numbers: log 100 minus log 4 equals log 25, which is not log 100 divided by log 4'><title>The quotient law checked on numbers: log 100 minus log 4 equals log 25, which is not log 100 divided by log 4</title><path d='M 14 16 L 14 118' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 14 16 L 24 16 M 14 118 L 24 118' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><text x='28' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log 100 - log 4</text><text x='330' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>two logarithms subtracted</text><rect x='18' y='47' width='290' height='26' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.09'/><text x='28' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log(100 / 4)</text><text x='330' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the quotient law</text><text x='28' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log 25</text><text x='330' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>not log 100 divided by log 4</text><text x='290' y='150' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>dividing the logarithms instead would give 3.321928, which is not a logarithm of anything here</text></svg>
caption: Subtracted outside, divided inside.

prompt: Using the quotient law shown above, what is $\log 12 - \log 3$ as a single logarithm?
explain: Subtracting outside divides inside, so it is $\log\frac{12}{3} = \log 4$. Dividing the two logarithms is a different calculation altogether.

text: 3. A number in front becomes a power

md:
$n \log a = \log a^{n}$. The coefficient climbs inside and becomes an index.
The part everyone misses: the power lands on **everything** inside. $3 \log 2x$ is $\log\left((2x)^{3}\right)$, and $(2x)^{3} = 8x^{3}$, so the answer is $\log 8x^{3}$. Leaving the $2$ alone gives $\log 2x^{3}$, which is a different expression.

alt: The power law applied to 3 log 2x: the whole of 2x is cubed, giving log 8x cubed, which is not the same as log 2x cubed.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 192' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='The power law applied to 3 log 2x: the whole of 2x is cubed, giving log 8x cubed, which is not the same as log 2x cubed'><title>The power law applied to 3 log 2x: the whole of 2x is cubed, giving log 8x cubed, which is not the same as log 2x cubed</title><path d='M 14 16 L 14 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 14 16 L 24 16 M 14 152 L 24 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><text x='28' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>3 log 2x</text><text x='330' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the number in front is a power</text><text x='28' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log (2x) cubed</text><text x='330' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the whole argument is cubed</text><rect x='18' y='81' width='290' height='26' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.09'/><text x='28' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log 8x cubed</text><text x='330' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>so the 2 is cubed as well</text><text x='28' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log 2x cubed</text><text x='330' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>this is a different expression</text><text x='290' y='184' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>the power belongs to everything inside the logarithm, coefficient included</text></svg>

title: Summer 2024, Unit 1, Question 6
md: Marks went here: writing $3\log 2x$ as a single logarithm, the majority forgot to cube the $2$. Write the bracket $(2x)^{3}$ before you expand it, every time.

prompt: Using the power law shown above, what is $2 \log 3x$ as a single logarithm?
explain: $(3x)^{2} = 9x^{2}$. The square lands on the $3$ as well as on the $x$, which is the step the Summer 2024 report says most candidates missed.

text: 4. Combining, one law at a time

md:
Express $\log a + 3\log b - 2\log c$ as a single logarithm.
**Step 1.** Coefficients first: $3\log b = \log b^{3}$ and $2\log c = \log c^{2}$.
**Step 2.** Add: $\log a + \log b^{3} = \log(ab^{3})$.
**Step 3.** Subtract: $\log(ab^{3}) - \log c^{2} = \log\frac{ab^{3}}{c^{2}}$.
The subtracted term goes **underneath**. Swapping which term goes on top and which goes underneath is the slip the 2025 report names.

alt: Combining log a plus 3 log b minus 2 log c into a single logarithm, one law at a time.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 192' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Combining log a plus 3 log b minus 2 log c into a single logarithm, one law at a time'><title>Combining log a plus 3 log b minus 2 log c into a single logarithm, one law at a time</title><path d='M 14 16 L 14 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 14 16 L 24 16 M 14 152 L 24 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><text x='28' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log a + 3 log b - 2 log c</text><text x='330' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>three terms, two with coefficients</text><rect x='18' y='47' width='290' height='26' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.09'/><text x='28' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log a + log b cubed - log c squared</text><text x='330' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>coefficients become powers first</text><text x='28' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log(a b cubed) - log c squared</text><text x='330' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the product law</text><text x='28' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log(a b cubed / c squared)</text><text x='330' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the quotient law</text><text x='290' y='184' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>coefficients first, then add, then subtract</text></svg>
caption: Coefficients, then add, then subtract.

prompt: In the combination shown above, the term $-2\log c$ became $-\log c^{2}$. Where does $c^{2}$ end up in the single logarithm?
explain: A subtracted logarithm divides, so $c^{2}$ goes underneath: $\log\frac{ab^{3}}{c^{2}}$.

text: 5. A lone number is a logarithm too

md:
The laws only combine logarithms, so a bare number has to be turned into one first. To base $10$, $1 = \log 10$ and $2 = \log 100$, because $10^{1} = 10$ and $10^{2} = 100$.
So $2 + \log x$ becomes $\log 100 + \log x = \log 100x$. Without that first line there is nothing the product law can act on.

alt: A constant rewritten as a logarithm: 2 equals log 100, so 2 plus log x becomes log 100x.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 192' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='A constant rewritten as a logarithm: 2 equals log 100, so 2 plus log x becomes log 100x'><title>A constant rewritten as a logarithm: 2 equals log 100, so 2 plus log x becomes log 100x</title><path d='M 14 16 L 14 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 14 16 L 24 16 M 14 152 L 24 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><rect x='18' y='13' width='290' height='26' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.09'/><text x='28' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>1 = log 10</text><text x='330' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>because 10 to the power 1 is 10</text><text x='28' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>2 = log 100</text><text x='330' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>because 10 squared is 100</text><text x='28' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>2 + log x = log 100 + log x</text><text x='330' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>now it is two logarithms</text><text x='28' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log 100x</text><text x='330' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>and the product law finishes it</text><text x='290' y='184' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>a lone number cannot be combined until it is written as a logarithm</text></svg>
caption: Write the number as a logarithm, then combine.

prompt: Using the rule shown above that $1 = \log 10$, what is $1 + \log x$ as a single logarithm?
explain: $1 = \log 10$, so $1 + \log x = \log 10 + \log x = \log 10x$. Dropping the $1$ altogether would leave $\log x$, which is a different number.

md:
Some questions want the opposite: one logarithm opened out into several. Use exactly the same three laws from right to left.
$\log(x^{3}y^{2})$ splits at the product into $\log x^{3} + \log y^{2}$, and then each power drops out in front: $3\log x + 2\log y$. A division inside becomes a minus, and a square root is a power of $\frac{1}{2}$.

alt: Expanding log of x cubed y squared into 3 log x plus 2 log y, using the product law and the power law backwards.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 158' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Expanding log of x cubed y squared into 3 log x plus 2 log y, using the product law and the power law backwards'><title>Expanding log of x cubed y squared into 3 log x plus 2 log y, using the product law and the power law backwards</title><path d='M 14 16 L 14 118' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 14 16 L 24 16 M 14 118 L 24 118' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><text x='28' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log(x cubed y squared)</text><text x='330' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>one logarithm of a product</text><rect x='18' y='47' width='290' height='26' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.09'/><text x='28' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= log x cubed + log y squared</text><text x='330' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the product law, backwards</text><text x='28' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>= 3 log x + 2 log y</text><text x='330' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>the power law, backwards</text><text x='290' y='150' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>the same three laws, read from right to left</text></svg>
caption: Split at the product, then bring each power down.

title: LOGS - Laws of Logs CCEA GCSE Further Mathematics
why: A Northern Ireland teacher running the three laws against this specification, in both directions.

prompt: Expanding as shown above, what is $\log(m^{4}n)$ written as separate logarithms?
explain: The product splits into a sum, then the power on $m$ drops out in front as a $4$.

md:
Once an equation reads $\log P = \log Q$, the logarithms can be dropped: $P = Q$. That is what the laws are usually for.
So $\log x + \log 4 = \log 20$ becomes $\log 4x = \log 20$, then $4x = 20$ and $x = 5$. Combine each side to one logarithm first; dropping them before that is what loses the marks.

alt: Equal logarithms have equal arguments: log x plus log 4 equals log 20 becomes 4x equals 20.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 580 192' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-label='Equal logarithms have equal arguments: log x plus log 4 equals log 20 becomes 4x equals 20'><title>Equal logarithms have equal arguments: log x plus log 4 equals log 20 becomes 4x equals 20</title><path d='M 14 16 L 14 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M 14 16 L 24 16 M 14 152 L 24 152' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='none' stroke-linejoin='round' stroke-linecap='round'/><text x='28' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log P = log Q</text><text x='330' y='34' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>two logarithms, equal</text><rect x='18' y='47' width='290' height='26' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.09'/><text x='28' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>P = Q</text><text x='330' y='68' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>so the arguments are equal</text><text x='28' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log x + log 4 = log 20</text><text x='330' y='102' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>combine the left side first</text><text x='28' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>log 4x = log 20, so 4x = 20</text><text x='330' y='136' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='start'>and 5 follows</text><text x='290' y='184' font-family='inherit' font-size='11.5' fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'>combine to one logarithm on each side, then drop the logarithms</text></svg>
caption: One logarithm each side, then drop them both.

prompt: Combining the left-hand side of $\log x + \log 4 = \log 20$ gives $\log 4x = \log 20$. What is $x$?
explain: Equal logarithms have equal arguments, so $4x = 20$ and $x = 5$. Writing $x + 4 = 20$ instead would give $16$.

md:
Combine logarithms with the product, quotient and power laws, in that order.
Apply a coefficient to the whole argument, the number inside included.
Put a subtracted term in the denominator, and a constant inside as a logarithm.
Expand one logarithm back into separate logarithms.
Read $\log P = \log Q$ as $P = Q$ and finish the equation.

The wording is "express as a single logarithm" for $2$ or $3$ marks, or "in terms of" given logarithms for $2$. The first mark is the coefficients written as powers; the last is one logarithm with the subtracted term underneath. Stuck? Deal with every coefficient first, then add, then subtract: the order never changes.
